entries.finding: A 2026 GRADE-based systematic review and dose-response meta-analysis of randomized trials found ginger supplementation was associated with a modest reduction in systolic blood pressure; certainty was rated low because of inconsistency.
The same 2026 synthesis found a smaller pooled reduction in diastolic blood pressure, but the authors emphasized limited robustness of the diastolic estimate and short trial durations.

In the 2026 ginger blood-pressure meta-analysis, larger reductions were observed in trials involving elevated baseline blood pressure, obesity, and doses at or above 2000 mg/day; these subgroup patterns do not establish an optimal clinical dose.
The 2026 ginger blood-pressure review reported significant pooled effects but substantial heterogeneity and short intervention periods, limiting confidence in definitive long-term conclusions.
A 2025 GRADE-based meta-analysis of 36 randomized trials found ginger supplementation significantly reduced waist circumference, while effects on body weight and BMI were not significant.
The 2025 ginger meta-analysis found a significant reduction in body-fat percentage, but did not find a significant improvement in major weight measures such as body weight or BMI.
The 2025 synthesis found ginger supplementation significantly increased serum adiponectin, an adipokine outcome, while the overall clinical relevance of the change remains uncertain.
The 2025 GRADE review concluded ginger did not appear effective for major weight indices including body weight and BMI, providing a boundary against broad weight-loss claims.
A 2026 systematic review and meta-analysis of randomized trials found no significant overall effect of cranberry consumption on C-reactive protein, with high heterogeneity across studies.
The same 2026 cranberry synthesis found no significant overall effect on interleukin-6, again with substantial between-study heterogeneity.

The 2026 cranberry meta-analysis reported subgroup signals in which cranberry was associated with increased CRP among obese participants or studies focused only on women, illustrating why the overall null result should not be simplified into universal anti-inflammatory benefit.
The 2026 review reported that powder-form cranberry interventions were associated with an increase in interleukin-6 in the relevant subgroup, underscoring formulation-specific uncertainty.
